extracted.intended_audience: stakeholders and commenters on EPA's endangerment finding (regulated entities, environmental groups, policymakers, and legal counsel)
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance and legal-scientific criteria for making an endangerment finding under Clean Air Act section 202(a) regarding the six well-mixed greenhouse gases, including how to define the pollutant, what evidence and projections to consider, and how to treat other climate forcers and uncertainties.

rubrics_metrics.name: Definition: Air pollution as aggregate of six well-mixed greenhouse gases
rubrics_metrics.description: Treating the air pollution as the aggregate of the well-mixed greenhouse gases is appropriate for the endangerment finding; these gases collectively are the primary driver of current and projected human-induced climate change.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This definition addresses the total, cumulative effect that the elevated concentrations of the six well-mixed greenhouse gases have on climate and on health, society and the environment. It is consistent with past EPA practice and CAA provisions that allow separate emissions with common properties to be treated as a class (e.g., particulate matter).

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of carbon dioxide equivalent metric
rubrics_metrics.description: Because of common properties, compare and sum the six gases on a carbon dioxide equivalent basis using global warming potentials published by the IPCC.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: EPA and international practice (UNFCCC, Clean Development Mechanism) use CO2-equivalent metrics to convert the six greenhouse gases into respective units; EPA's inventory and reporting rules accept this approach.

rubrics_metrics.name: Consideration of future scenarios and long atmospheric lifetimes
rubrics_metrics.description: Future atmospheric concentrations are influenced by present-day and near-term emissions due to long atmospheric lifetimes of the six greenhouse gases; most no-mitigation scenarios project increasing emissions and concentrations, with CO2 remaining dominant.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Model projections (e.g., IPCC summaries) show warming through the 21st century varying by emissions scenario and climate sensitivity (e.g., 1.8 to 4.0 °C by century end with wider uncertainty). Scenarios indicate CO2 will be the largest contributor to radiative forcing; aerosol projections are more uncertain due to short lifetimes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Exclusion/inclusion criteria for other climate forcers (black carbon, CFCs, NF3, water vapor, tropospheric ozone)
rubrics_metrics.description: Other substances affecting climate may be important but are not included in this finding because they differ in properties (e.g., not well-mixed, short-lived, controlled under other regimes, or poorly quantified).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Black carbon: aerosol particle, short atmospheric lifetime (~week), not a greenhouse gas and part of PM; significant scientific uncertainties and metric/comparison issues. Ozone-depleting substances: being phased out under Montreal Protocol so assessment literature focuses on the six gases. NF3: included in reporting but overall forcing magnitude not well quantified, so excluded for now. Water vapor: direct anthropogenic emissions negligible, short residence time, radiative forcing per mass less than CO2. Tropospheric ozone: not long-lived/well-mixed and forms from precursors; deserves separate evaluation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Reliance on multiple lines of evidence for attribution
rubrics_metrics.description: Attribution of recent warming to anthropogenic greenhouse gases is based on multiple lines of evidence: basic physical understanding, indirect historical estimates, and climate model simulations that cannot reproduce observed warming without anthropogenic forcings.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Also consider that sum of solar and volcanic forcing over past half-century would likely have produced cooling; use models, observational records, and paleoclimate reconstructions together to support attribution.

rubrics_metrics.name: Treatment of short-term variability vs long-term trends
rubrics_metrics.description: Short-term pauses or decade-scale variability in temperature records should not be interpreted as evidence that warming is not occurring; year-to-year variability can mask long-term trends.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate long-term trends (e.g., 30-year records) and corroborate with independent observations (sea ice loss, glacier retreat, snow cover reduction, earlier plant blooming, ice sheet melt) rather than rely on very short time windows.

rubrics_metrics.name: Evidence consistency and correction for observational biases
rubrics_metrics.description: Consider potential biases (urbanization, instrument siting, observation methods) but recognize literature shows many biases have been corrected or are random and cancel out regionally; multiple surface and satellite records producing similar results increases confidence.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use corroborating indicators (cryosphere changes, phenology, sea level) and relevant assessment literature to assess legitimacy of temperature records.

rubrics_metrics.name: Endangerment determination based on total weight of scientific evidence
rubrics_metrics.description: The Administrator must use judgment and base a positive endangerment finding on the total weight of scientific evidence regarding risks and impacts across all climate-sensitive elements of public health and welfare; no bright-line quantitative threshold is required.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Consider a range of risk categories and their potential magnitudes over time; weigh threats and potential benefits across categories and regions in aggregate to judge whether risks amount to endangerment.

rubrics_metrics.name: Evaluation across multiple risk categories (public health and welfare)
rubrics_metrics.description: Assess how elevated greenhouse gas concentrations may affect major risk categories, including human health, air quality, food production and agriculture, forestry, water resources, sea level rise and coastal areas, the energy sector, infrastructure and settlements, and ecosystems and wildlife.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Recognize that nature and severity of impacts vary by category, region, and time; not all risks can be equally quantified or compared with uniform metrics, so exercise judgment.

rubrics_metrics.name: Cumulative impact approach vs incremental/domestic-only approach
rubrics_metrics.description: Endangerment analysis should consider the cumulative impact of all sources on atmospheric concentrations, not an incremental or domestic-only assessment that isolates only domestic contributions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Text of CAA and legislative history support judging air pollution by cumulative impacts; isolating only domestic-origin molecules would be an artificial construct rejected by courts and Congress.

rubrics_metrics.name: Focus on impacts occurring in the United States for endangerment
rubrics_metrics.description: Core judgments for endangerment focus on impacts inside the United States and effects on the U.S. population, even when the pollution is part of a global atmospheric pool.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Defining air pollution as global concentrations is consistent with protecting the Nation's air resources, since the air over the U.S. is part of the global pool and impacts cannot be meaningfully isolated from global concentrations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Statutory interpretation: contribution test versus endangerment
rubrics_metrics.description: CAA section 202(a) differentiates between determining endangerment (which looks at the pollutant and its impacts) and determining what controls are required; the contribution test in section 202(a) concerns whether emissions from the relevant domestic source category (e.g., new motor vehicles) cause or contribute to the air pollution.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Effectiveness of potential regulatory controls is not a relevant factor in making the endangerment determination; commenters' concerns about extra-territoriality do not negate EPA's authority to make an endangerment finding.

rubrics_metrics.name: Treat uncertainty transparently but proceed when evidence is robust
rubrics_metrics.description: Acknowledge significant scientific uncertainties (e.g., aerosols, black carbon effects, NF3 forcing, water vapor contributions), but recognize that uncertainty does not preclude finding endangerment when the total evidence and risk assessment justify it.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: EPA will continue to track evolving science and explains specific reasons for exclusion or cautious treatment of certain substances where understanding or quantification is limited.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of assessment literature and major scientific reports (e.g., IPCC)
rubrics_metrics.description: Rely on IPCC and other major assessment literature to summarize climate model results, global projections, warming ranges, and state of scientific understanding.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assessment reports provide consistent bases for projections (e.g., warming rates through 2030 are less sensitive to scenario choice; end-of-century warming varies with scenario and sensitivity). Use these reports to inform projections and uncertainties.

rubrics_metrics.name: Consideration of physical attributes such as residence time in inclusion decisions
rubrics_metrics.description: Decisions on inclusion of substances in the defined air pollution consider properties like being well-mixed and long-lived versus short residence time (e.g., black carbon ~1 week, water vapor days).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Well-mixed, long-lived gases are appropriate for aggregate treatment; short-lived, spatially/seasonally variable aerosols present comparison metric challenges and are treated differently or discussed separately.
